questions.question: What does `__add__` let you do, and what expression triggers it?
options: It defines what `a + b` means for your objects; `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`.
It adds a method to the class at runtime.
questions.explanation: `__add__` is operator overloading for `+`. Writing `a + b` invokes `a.__add__(b)`, so you can define addition for a Fraction or Vector naturally. Each operator has its own dunder, for example `__sub__` for `-` and `__mul__` for `*`.

questions.scenario: You write a function `def total_area(shapes):` that loops and calls `shape.area()` on each item, where shapes may be circles, squares, or triangles.
questions.question: Which idea makes this one function work for every shape type?
options: Polymorphism: each class implements `area()` its own way, and the caller uses the shared interface without knowing the concrete type.
Operator overloading of the plus sign.
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets objects of different types respond to the same method call in their own way. The function depends only on the shared `area()` interface, so adding a new shape needs no change to `total_area`. This is the open-closed benefit of polymorphism.
questions.misconception: The function does not branch on type. It relies on each type honoring a common interface, which is the point of polymorphism.

questions.question: Python does not support classic method overloading (same name, different signatures). What is the common Pythonic substitute?
options: Overloading is fully supported with type annotations.
Using a different class per signature.
Defining the method twice; the second wins.
Default arguments or `*args` and `**kwargs` so one method handles varied inputs.
questions.explanation: Defining a method twice just replaces the first with the second in Python. Instead, you write one method that adapts using default parameters or variadic arguments. True compile-time overloading does not exist in Python.
